extracted.intended_audience: patent scholars, policymakers, patent office officials, and IP practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Comparative analysis of the design, procedures, and outcomes of post-grant patent review systems (U.S. IPR/PGR, EPO opposition, German nullity) to evaluate how specific design features affect speed, cost, fairness, and invalidation outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and duration of review
rubrics_metrics.description: When review is offered, and how long it takes (first window = within nine months after grant; second window = after the first nine months; life-of-the-patent reviews available anytime). U.S. PGR completes ~12–18 months after institution; IPR final determination within 12 months (plus up to 6 months extension); EPO opposition historically ~24 months, aiming for 15 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing affects incentives to challenge (stakes higher in second-window-less systems), interaction with litigation (stay/injunction gap), and whether review substitutes for or complements litigation. Short, predictable timelines (fixed time frames) contributed to IPR's popularity; EPO reforms aim to shorten pendency while preserving right to be heard and amendment rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who can initiate and participate
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether proceedings are inter partes (third parties other than the patentee can initiate) or ex parte (only patentee and patent office). Example: IPR and PGR are inter partes (initiated by anyone but the patent owner for PGR), whereas some EPO/German limitation/revocation or U.S. reissue proceedings can only be initiated by patentees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Who may initiate affects accessibility, pooling of resources (e.g., Unified Patents), and the public-good aspects of invalidation. Inter partes availability supports third-party challenges; exclusive patentee-initiated procedures are tools for patentees to tune scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds of challenge / scope of review
rubrics_metrics.description: Which statutory or doctrinal bases can be raised in the proceeding. Example: PGR can challenge any grounds of patentability except best mode; IPR limited to anticipation/obviousness based on patents and printed publications; EPO opposition grounds include article 100(a)–(c) (novelty, inventive step, sufficiency, added matter), excluding 'clarity' in some contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scope shapes how thorough/expansive review can be and what evidence is relevant; broader grounds (PGR/EPO) allow more complete validity assessment, while narrower grounds (IPR) constrain challenges but may streamline proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-institution filter / institution decision standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Threshold for the tribunal to institute review based on the petition. IPR requires showing a 'reasonable likelihood of prevailing' on at least one claim; PGR requires 'more likely than not' that at least one challenged claim is unpatentable. EPO opposition has no formal separate institution stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A pre-institution filter affects selection bias (instituted cases are more likely invalid), inflating observed invalidation rates for reviewed petitions versus all challenged patents. SAS Institute requires PTAB to institute on 'all claims or none' (no partial institution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The interpretive standard applied to claims in the proceeding and its consistency with litigation. The PTO changed claim interpretation during IPRs to make it consistent with the standard applied in litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harmonizing claim construction between PTAB and courts reduces divergent outcomes and downstream uncertainty. Differences in construction can amplify bifurcation issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment practice and patentee rights to amend
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether and how patentees can amend claims during/post proceedings. EPO allows patentee amendments with conditions and has an established practice of maintaining patents in amended form; U.S. IPR historically limited amendment rights, with Aqua Products and later PTO changes altering the standard for amended claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generous amendment rights (EPO) can protect patentees and encourage consolidation, but may lengthen proceedings; restrictive amendment practice (US IPR) reduces opportunities for patentees and creates tension over uncertainty and the value of surviving claims. Burden of proof for amended claims and requirement to consider the entire record (Aqua Products) are relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serial challenges and consolidation of petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether multiple, successive challenges against the same patent are allowed or whether opposition periods/centralized procedures consolidate challenges (EPO opposition encourages single-window challenges; U.S. second-window design makes consolidation harder, enabling serial IPR petitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consolidation reduces duplicative cost and uncertainty; serial challenges can multiply delay and cost and create strategic behavior. Design options include encouraging joinder or adding PTAB resources (e.g., extra panel member) to handle subsequent challengers without delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination between infringement and invalidity proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: How post-grant reviews interact with parallel litigation (stay practice, bifurcation). U.S. courts often stay infringement proceedings when IPR is instituted (high stay rate ~80% in parallel cases), whereas German courts rarely stay, creating an 'injunction gap.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordination affects whether post-grant review substitutes for litigation or complements it; high stay rates can avoid 'invalid but infringed' outcomes and reduce injunction gaps, whereas low stay rates can produce injunctions later found invalid, harming defendants and incentivizing settlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjudication rate / merits-based decision rate
rubrics_metrics.description: Share of petitions that result in a merits decision (institution leads to higher adjudication). EPO opposition has highest share of merits-based adjudication; U.S. IPR's institution decision provides early clarification and increases chance of merits decisions; German nullity has lower adjudication rate due to longer process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher adjudication rates mean the forum resolves validity questions on the merits more often; lower rates can leave questions unresolved or push them to courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidation rates and selection effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed rates of partial or full invalidation (e.g., 81% of reviewed IPR claims canceled; when considering challenged patents rather than reviewed ones, US IPR invalidation rate is ~26%; EPO challenged patent invalidation ~63%; German ~28%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported invalidation rates can be misleading without accounting for selection bias (pre-institution filter) and whether rates are measured at petition-level vs patent-level. Use consistent denominators (reviewed vs challenged patents) when comparing venues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed and predictability
rubrics_metrics.description: How quickly the forum reaches key procedural milestones and final decisions, and how predictable timing is (e.g., IPR has strict schedule and predictable institution decision within ~6 months; EPO reforms aim to increase predictability and shorten pendency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speed supports substitutive function (reduces parallel litigation consequences), reduces injunction gaps, and makes the forum attractive to users; predictability helps parties plan enforcement and defense strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery and evidentiary rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Scope of discovery and acceptable evidence in the proceeding. IPR introduced evidentiary guidelines and (relative to predecessors) expanded discovery; PTAB and examiners rely more on non-patent literature in IPRs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discovery rules influence costs, the ability to develop prior art, and the thoroughness of review. More discovery can make administrative review more like litigation (costly) but can improve accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preclusive effects / estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether and how final decisions in post-grant review preclude subsequent validity challenges in district courts or the ITC (e.g., 35 U.S.C. §325(e) precludes petitioner from asserting any ground 'raised or reasonably could have raised' in PGR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preclusion affects strategic behavior, settlement incentives, and the public-good problem (deterring duplicate challenges). Strong preclusion can encourage full-lottery challenges early; limited preclusion may invite serial litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource allocation and procedural centralization
rubrics_metrics.description: How the forum organizes expertise and staff (e.g., EPO concentrated oppositions on a central pool of experienced examiners; opposition divisions restructured to avoid prior-examiner involvement), and how resource decisions affect impartiality and timeliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralizing expertise and separating examining and opposition functions can improve impartiality and efficiency; resourcing affects ability to meet strict timelines and handle complex cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bifurcation consequences and injunction gap
rubrics_metrics.description: Effects of separating infringement and validity decisions (bifurcated systems) including 'invalid but infringed' outcomes and the resulting injunction gap (German median injunction gap ~13.5 months).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bifurcation may speed infringement resolution but can disadvantage defendants and smaller parties, increase costs, and create incentives to settle; possible mitigations include flexible injunctions, conditions on stays, bonding, or other measures to reduce harm during injunction gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access, cost, and procedural fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: The cost of participating in dual proceedings and the distributional effects on small or resource-constrained parties and foreign firms. Dual proceedings and extra complexity disproportionately impact smaller parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design choices should consider fairness and access (e.g., simplified procedures, support for smaller parties, facilitation of joinder) to avoid tilting playing field toward well-resourced actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidation and single-window effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the system aggregates challenges into a single proceeding (EPO first-window opposition consolidates challenges) versus allowing fragmented multiple challenges (common in second-window systems like U.S. IPR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single-window consolidation reduces duplicative effort and conflicting outcomes; absent a time-limited opposition window, designers may need procedural tools to encourage consolidation without delaying proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrics for evaluating post-grant systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested performance-based metrics include adjudication rate, invalidation rate (reviewed vs challenged), time to merits-decision, stay/bifurcation-related outcomes, settlement rates, and procedural fairness indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons across systems should use these common metrics and adjust for selection bias, different denominators, and jurisdictional rules to assess whether reviews are substituting for litigation or just adding cost/delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional design features that increase uptake
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific procedural design choices that affected usage: fixed time frames, strict schedules, expanded discovery, evidentiary guidelines, pre-institution filters, and the ability to stay parallel litigation. These features made IPR more popular than its predecessors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small design details can have large impacts on uptake and outcomes; policymakers should weigh tradeoffs (e.g., speed vs amendment rights) when reforming procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal and finality mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: How decisions can be appealed and the finality of PTAB/EPO/court determinations; interactions with district court and ITC processes (e.g., preclusive effects) shape the broader litigation landscape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appealability affects confidence in administrative outcomes and influences courts' willingness to stay infringement proceedings; designers should ensure clarity about finality and standards of review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of non-patent literature and examination complementarities
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that PTAB relies more on non-patent literature in IPRs than examiners do during initial examination, suggesting post-grant reviews can catch errors missed at examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding why IPRs rely on different evidence types could inform improvements to pre-grant examination procedures, reducing downstream correction needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural rules to promote timeliness without sacrificing rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples from EPO reforms: stricter limits on time extensions, parallel processing, limiting intermediate office actions (one intermediate action = summons to oral proceedings), setting deadlines for last submissions, and specialized examiner pools to reduce pendency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reforms can shorten pendency for 'straightforward' cases while preserving the patentee's right to be heard and amendment capabilities for complex cases; exceptional handling for complex matters should be retained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of national enforcement structure on post-grant design
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPO issues a unitary grant that requires national validation for enforcement, affecting incentives to challenge during the first window; German court speed and national nullity procedures produce different interaction dynamics than centralized administrative review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers must consider enforcement architecture (central grant + national enforcement vs single national patent) since it affects strategic timing and the value of centralized opposition periods.
